bai.moTa: At high speeds, the slice of “now” itself tilts
bai.yChinh: The speed of light is the same for every observer. For that to hold, time and space must mix into one another when we change frames: moving clocks run slow, moving rulers contract, and observers in relative motion disagree on what counts as “at the same time.” On a spacetime diagram, changing frames is a “hyperbolic rotation”: light rays stay put while events slide along invariant hyperbolas.
bai.conSo.2: **0.976 c**: the speed of an object fired at 0.8 c from a ship already flying at 0.8 c.
bai.conSo.3: **10.9 years and 6.6 years**: the two twins after a round trip to Alpha Centauri at 0.8 c.
bai.conSo.4: **10.4 km**: average distance traveled by a 0.998 c muon, instead of 659 m.
bai.conSo.5: **7.2 microseconds per day**: how much a GPS satellite clock loses because of its orbital speed.
bai.hieuDung: **Time dilation does not mean a clock is broken.** Every process aboard the ship (clocks, heartbeats, particle decay) runs normally for those on the ship. What differs is that two frames slice spacetime into different sheets of “now,” so they measure different time intervals between two events. What every frame agrees on is the interval s² and the proper time along each world line.
bai.nguon: Muon lifetime 2.1969811 µs and proton mass 0.93827208816 GeV: PDG and CODATA 2018. Atmospheric muons: Rossi and Hall 1941, Phys. Rev. 59, 223. Muons in the CERN storage ring: Bailey et al. 1977, Nature 268, 301. LHC beam energy 6.5 TeV: CERN 2015–2018 run. GPS satellite speed 3.874 km/s: orbital radius 26,560 km. Alpha Centauri distance 4.37 light-years. All numerical values in this lesson are recomputed in kiem-tra/kiem-lorentz.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: State Einstein’s two postulates and see why they force time to be relative.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Derive the factor γ from a light clock and use it to calculate time dilation and length contraction.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Draw a moving observer’s ct′ and x′ axes on a Minkowski diagram and read off that observer’s “now.”
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Apply the Lorentz transformation and the velocity-addition formula, and recognize the invariance of the interval s².

bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
On screen is the familiar spacetime diagram from Lesson 4 and Lesson 5: the horizontal axis is $x$, the vertical axis is $ct$, and depth is $y$. A flash of light goes off at the origin, spreading outward as the yellow {{nón ánh sáng|light cone}}. The blue straight line is a spaceship flying past the flash at $0{,}6\,c$.

In 1905, Einstein built the entire theory of special relativity on two statements, known as the two {{tiên đề|postulates}}:

1. **The laws of physics are the same in every {{khung quán tính|inertial frame}}.** No experiment performed inside a closed spaceship coasting at constant velocity can tell whether the ship is “truly” at rest or moving.
2. **The speed of light in vacuum is the same for every observer**, regardless of how the source or observer moves: $c = 299\,792{,}458$ km/s.

The two green rings show the wavefront of the flash **at the same time according to the laboratory**: circles centered on the stationary observer. The two blue rings show the wavefront **at the same time according to the ship**. All four rings lie on **the very same cone**.

> [Thử ngay] Switch to the ship’s frame. The whole diagram tilts, yet the light cone stays unchanged. Now the blue rings become circles centered on the ship: each observer sees light spreading equally in all directions around them. Back in the laboratory frame, drag the blue dot near the bottom of the ship’s world line to change its speed: the blue rings deform accordingly while staying on the cone.
> [[View from the ship|tau]] [[View from the lab|lab]] [[Ship at 0.9 c|b9]]

Here is the seeming paradox: two observers moving relative to each other both stand at the center of the same expanding sphere of light. That is possible only if the two observers **do not share the same “now.”** Every result in this lesson follows from that single fact.

+++ Go deeper: why ordinary velocity addition fails for light
According to Galileo and Newton, if a ship flies at $v$ and fires a bullet forward at $u$, the bullet travels at $u + v$ relative to the ground. Applied to light, a beam emitted from the ship ought to travel at $c + v$. Experiment says otherwise. The Michelson–Morley experiment (1887) showed that the measured speed of light does not change despite Earth’s motion. And the fact that light from a moving source still travels at $c$ rather than $c + v$ was confirmed using light from binary stars (de Sitter, 1913) and gamma rays from pions moving near $c$ (Alväger et al., 1964).

Einstein chose to trust postulate 2 and revise how coordinates transform. The new rule (the Lorentz transformation, step 5) preserves postulate 1 because it takes the exact same form in every inertial frame, and preserves postulate 2 because it maps the light cone onto itself. The price we pay: time is no longer universal.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Here are two identical {{đồng hồ ánh sáng|light clocks}}. Each consists of two parallel mirrors separated by a distance $h$ along the $y$ (depth) direction. A pulse of light bounces back and forth between the mirrors; each return to the lower mirror counts as one “tick.” The colored ribbon is the world strip of the two mirrors, and the zigzag yellow line is the world line of the light pulse.

The white clock sits at rest in the laboratory: its light goes straight there and straight back, taking $2h/c$ per tick. The blue clock rides aboard the ship. Seen from the laboratory, its light must follow a longer, diagonal path while still traveling at speed $c$. Each tick therefore **takes longer**:

$$ \Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta\tau, \qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} $$

Here $\Delta\tau$ is the time between ticks measured by that clock itself (proper time), $\Delta t$ is the time measured in the laboratory, and $\gamma$ is the {{hệ số Lorentz|Lorentz factor}}. At $0{,}6\,c$, for example, $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0{,}36} = 1/0{,}8 = 1{,}25$. While the ship’s clock ticks 4 times, the laboratory clock ticks 5 times. This is {{giãn thời gian|time dilation}}.

| $v/c$ | 0.1 | 0.5 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 0.9 | 0.99 | 0.999 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\gamma$ | 1.005 | 1.155 | 1.25 | 1.667 | 2.294 | 7.089 | 22.37 |

> [Thử ngay] The rising green glass sheet marks “now” in the current viewing frame; the tick counts of both clocks appear in the data panel. Listen: each tick of the laboratory clock plays a low tone on the left, and each tick of the ship’s clock plays a high tone on the right; at $0{,}6\,c$, the tones on the right come 1.25 times less often. Drag the blue dot on the ship clock’s line to vary the speed. Then switch to the ship’s frame: now it is the laboratory clock that runs slow. Time dilation is **symmetric**.
> [[Ship at 0.6 c|b6]] [[Ship at 0.8 c|b8]] [[View from the ship|tau]] [[Back to the lab|lab]]

> [Lưu ý] The mirror spacing $h$ = 1 unit is drawn on the scale of the whole diagram so the light path is easy to see. A real clock is far smaller, and the result does not depend on $h$. The ticks sound in step with the light pulse in the model, slowed down so your ear can follow them: one tick of the stationary clock lasts about 1.8 seconds.

+++ Go deeper: deriving γ line by line with the Pythagorean theorem
Follow half a tick of the ship’s clock as seen from the laboratory, letting $\Delta t$ be the duration of one full tick.

1. In half a tick, the light pulse travels a distance $c\,\Delta t/2$ (postulate 2: its speed is still $c$).
2. Meanwhile, the ship moves sideways by $v\,\Delta t/2$.
3. The mirrors are separated by $h$ perpendicular to the motion. Transverse lengths do not contract (if they did, two identical clocks passing each other would each find the other’s mirror spacing shorter, a contradiction).
4. By the Pythagorean theorem: $(c\,\Delta t/2)^2 = h^2 + (v\,\Delta t/2)^2$.
5. Rearranging: $(\Delta t/2)^2\,(c^2 - v^2) = h^2$, so $\Delta t = \dfrac{2h}{\sqrt{c^2 - v^2}} = \dfrac{2h/c}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$.
6. Aboard the ship, light goes straight back and forth, so $\Delta\tau = 2h/c$. Dividing gives $\Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta\tau$.

At everyday speeds $\gamma$ is extremely close to 1: an airliner at 900 km/h has $\gamma - 1 \approx 3{,}5 \times 10^{-13}$. That is why nobody noticed before 1905.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Adjust the ship’s velocity so that **γ = 2**: for every single tick of the ship’s clock, the laboratory clock ticks twice.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: $\gamma = 2$ means $\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 1/2$, so $v = \tfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\,c \approx 0{,}87\,c$. Read the current γ in the data panel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Two flashes A and B go off at $x = -3$ and $x = +3$, **at the same time** $t = 0$ in the laboratory frame. An observer standing midway between them ($x = 0$, white line) receives light from both at the exact same moment, $t = 3$. The green glass sheet is the laboratory’s “now”: horizontal, containing both A and B.

The spaceship passes the midpoint just as the two flashes go off. Because it rushes toward B, it meets the light from B first ($t = 1{,}875$) and from A later ($t = 7{,}5$). Observers on the ship know they sit equidistant from the two flash sites and that light travels at the same speed $c$ from both directions (postulate 2). They must conclude: **B flashed before A**.

The blue glass sheet is the ship’s “now”: the plane $t' = 0$, or $ct = (v/c)\,x$. It **tilts** at the same angle as the ct′ axis, but in the opposite sense—symmetric across the 45° light ray. Event B lies below this sheet (in the ship’s past), while A lies above it (in its future).

> [Thử ngay] Switch to the ship’s frame: the blue sheet becomes horizontal and the green sheet tilts. Bring the ship to rest: the two sheets coincide. In the laboratory frame, drag the blue dot on the ct′ axis and watch the blue sheet tilt along with it. A chime sounds whenever light from either flash reaches the midpoint observer or the ship.
> [[View from the ship|tau]] [[Back to the lab|lab]] [[Bring ship to rest|b0]] [[Ship at 0.6 c|b6]]

> [Ví dụ] At $0{,}6\,c$ ($\gamma = 1{,}25$), according to the ship’s clocks, B flashes at $t' = -\gamma (v/c)\,x_B/c = -2{,}25$ and A flashes at $t' = +2{,}25$. The two flashes are 4.5 time units apart.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] Compare this with Lesson 4: a Galilean frame change tilts world lines while every sheet of “now” **stays horizontal**. Here, the sheet of “now” itself tilts. This is the {{đồng thời tương đối|relativity of simultaneity}}, the core break between Newton and Einstein. At low speeds the tilt is tiny, so it escapes everyday notice.

+++ Go deeper: why the ship’s “now” is the line ct = βx
Observers on the ship synchronize clocks using light (Einstein’s protocol): send a flash in both directions from the center of the ship; equidistant ends must receive it at the same ship time. Seen from the laboratory, the rear end moves forward to meet the light and receives it early, while the front end moves away and receives it late.

With $c = 1$, emit the flash from the origin at $t = 0$, with the ends initially at $x = \pm a$ moving at speed $\beta$. The front receives the flash at $t_1 = a/(1 - \beta)$ and the rear at $t_2 = a/(1 + \beta)$. By definition, these two reception events are “simultaneous” for the ship. Connecting them gives slope $\dfrac{t_1 - t_2}{x_1 - x_2} = \beta$. Thus the ship’s lines of simultaneity satisfy $ct = \beta x + \text{hằng số}$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Adjust the ship’s velocity so that, according to the ship’s clocks, flash B occurs **6** time units before flash A.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: In the ship’s frame, the flashes are separated by $\Delta t' = 2\gamma\beta L$ with $L = 3$. You need $\gamma\beta = 1$, so $v = c/\sqrt 2 \approx 0{,}71\,c$. Check both $t'$ values in the data panel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Length contraction: two ways to slice a strip
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Aboard the ship is a ruler of length $L_0 = 4$ units as measured at rest on the ship. $L_0$ is called its **proper length**. In spacetime, a ruler is not a single line segment but a **strip**: the blue world strip bounded by the world lines of its two ends.

The “length of a ruler” means the distance between its two ends **measured at the same time**. Because observers disagree on what “at the same time” means, each frame slices the strip differently:

- The laboratory slices with its horizontal “now” sheet, getting the **green** segment of length $L_0/\gamma$.
- The ship slices with its tilted “now” sheet, getting the **pink** segment of length $L_0$ as measured on the ship.

$$ L = \frac{L_0}{\gamma} $$

At $0{,}6\,c$, $L = 4/1{,}25 = 3{,}2$. At $0{,}8\,c$, $L = 4/1{,}667 = 2{,}4$. This is {{co độ dài|length contraction}}. It occurs only along the direction of motion; transverse dimensions (such as $y$) remain unchanged.

> [Thử ngay] A ruler painted in four segments lies on the $t = 0$ “now” of the current viewing frame. Drag the blue dot on the ct′ axis to change speed: the ruler shortens, all four segments contracting together. Switch to the ship’s frame: the world strip stands upright, the pink segment becomes horizontal at 4 segments long, and the ruler shows its full length of 4; meanwhile, the green segment tilts, connecting two events that are **not simultaneous** in the ship’s frame.
> [[View from the ship|tau]] [[Back to the lab|lab]] [[Ship at 0.8 c|b8]] [[Ship at 0.6 c|b6]]

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “The ruler is physically crushed, its atoms squeezed together.” No. No force compresses the ruler. The two segments are simply two different cross-sections of **the same world strip** in spacetime, much as slicing a log at an angle gives a longer cross-section than slicing it straight across. Length contraction is a direct consequence of the relativity of simultaneity.

+++ Go deeper: deriving L = L₀/γ from the diagram
Set $c = 1$. The ruler’s ends stay at $x' = 0$ and $x' = L_0$ for all $t'$. Apply the Lorentz transformation $x' = \gamma(x - \beta t)$ to both ends at the same laboratory time $t$:

$$ L_0 = x'_2 - x'_1 = \gamma\big[(x_2 - \beta t) - (x_1 - \beta t)\big] = \gamma\,(x_2 - x_1) = \gamma L $$

The time $t$ cancels because both ends are measured **simultaneously** in the laboratory, leaving $L = L_0/\gamma$. Reversing the roles (measuring a ruler at rest in the lab from the ship) likewise gives $L_0/\gamma$: length contraction is symmetric too.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Adjust the ship’s velocity so the laboratory measures the ruler to be **3** segments long (while its proper length remains 4).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: $L = L_0/\gamma$ requires $\gamma = 4/3$, or $v = \tfrac{\sqrt 7}{4}\,c \approx 0{,}66\,c$. Read the measured length in the data panel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Now let us put everything together in a single picture. The faint white grid is the laboratory coordinate grid; the blue grid belongs to the ship. Each cell of the ship’s grid is a rhombus: the ct′ axis tilts toward the light ray, and the x′ axis tilts upward toward the same light ray. Transforming coordinates from one frame to the other is the {{phép biến đổi Lorentz|Lorentz transformation}}:

$$ ct' = \gamma\,(ct - \beta x), \qquad x' = \gamma\,(x - \beta\,ct), \qquad y' = y, \qquad \beta = \frac{v}{c} $$

The soft purple curves are the hyperbolas $-c^2t^2 + x^2 = $ −9, −4, −1, 1, 4, 9. The transformation preserves the **spacetime interval**:

$$ s^2 = -c^2t^2 + x^2 + y^2 = -c^2t'^2 + x'^2 + y'^2 $$

so each event slides only along its own hyperbola. Unit tick marks in every frame lie on these hyperbolas: the mark 1 on the ct′ axis sits on the hyperbola $s^2 = -1$, at $\gamma$ times the height of the laboratory’s mark on the diagram.

> [Thử ngay] Click “Rock back and forth” and watch the three sample events P, Q, R: their coordinates change continuously while the $s^2$ value beside each stays fixed, and the two light rays remain in place. Or drag the blue dot near the bottom of the ct′ axis: the blue grid closes toward the light ray like a pair of scissors as tick marks 1, 2, 3, 4 slide along their hyperbolas. Hover over P, Q, R to compare their coordinates in both frames.
> [[Rock back and forth|lac]] [[View from the ship|tau]] [[Back to the lab|lab]] [[Ship at 0.9 c|b9]]

### Ordinary rotation versus hyperbolic rotation

Lesson 3 treated time as another dimension. Rotating an ordinary plane preserves $x^2 + y^2$ and uses $\cos$ and $\sin$ of the rotation angle. Changing inertial frames preserves $-c^2t^2 + x^2$ and uses $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ of the **rapidity** $\varphi$:

$$ \beta = \tanh\varphi, \quad \gamma = \cosh\varphi, \quad \gamma\beta = \sinh\varphi $$

For example, $0{,}6\,c$ corresponds to $\varphi = \ln 2 \approx 0{,}693$, and $0{,}8\,c$ corresponds to $\varphi = \ln 3 \approx 1{,}099$. That minus sign in $s^2$ is what distinguishes spacetime from ordinary four-dimensional space.

+++ Go deeper: proving s² is invariant
Set $c = 1$ and substitute $t' = \gamma(t - \beta x)$ and $x' = \gamma(x - \beta t)$:

$$ -t'^2 + x'^2 = \gamma^2\big[-(t - \beta x)^2 + (x - \beta t)^2\big] $$

Expanding inside the brackets gives $-t^2 + 2\beta t x - \beta^2 x^2 + x^2 - 2\beta x t + \beta^2 t^2 = (1 - \beta^2)(x^2 - t^2)$. Multiplying by $\gamma^2 = 1/(1 - \beta^2)$ yields $-t^2 + x^2$. Since $y$ is unchanged, adding $y^2$ to both sides leaves them equal.

Conversely, one can prove that any linear coordinate transformation preserving $s^2$ (and the direction of time) must be a Lorentz transformation, possibly combined with a spatial rotation. Einstein’s two postulates are equivalent to this requirement.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The spaceship (blue) flies at $u = 0{,}8\,c$ relative to the laboratory. As it passes the origin, it fires an object (pink) forward at $v = 0{,}8\,c$ **relative to the ship**. According to Newton, the object would travel at $1{,}6\,c$: the dashed red line, tilted past 45°, outside the light cone. Nature does not allow that. The correct formula is:

$$ w = \frac{u + v}{1 + uv/c^2} = \frac{0{,}8 + 0{,}8}{1 + 0{,}64}\,c \approx 0{,}976\,c $$

The label at the tip of each world line gives its speed **measured in the current viewing frame**, read directly from the line’s slope.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the pink dot on the object’s world line to vary its launch speed: even pushed all the way, it only ever approaches the yellow light line. Switch to the ship’s frame: the ship stands still, the object flies at its launch speed, and the laboratory recedes at $0{,}8\,c$. Then have the ship fire a beam of light: in every frame, the label reads 1 c.
> [[View from the ship|tau]] [[Back to the lab|lab]] [[Fire a light beam|as]] [[Launch at 0.8 c|v8]]

- When $u$ and $v$ are small, the denominator is nearly 1 and the formula reduces to Newton’s $u + v$.
- When $v = c$, $w = (u + c)/(1 + u/c) = c$: combining light with any frame speed still gives $c$, matching postulate 2.
- Two speeds below $c$ always combine to a speed below $c$.

+++ Go deeper: adding velocities means adding rapidities
Two collinear Lorentz transformations in succession (from lab to ship, then from ship to object) form a single Lorentz transformation. In the language of hyperbolic rotations, their rotation angles simply add: $\varphi_w = \varphi_u + \varphi_v$.

Using the hyperbolic tangent addition identity, $\tanh(\varphi_u + \varphi_v) = \dfrac{\tanh\varphi_u + \tanh\varphi_v}{1 + \tanh\varphi_u \tanh\varphi_v}$. Substituting $\tanh\varphi = v/c$ yields the velocity-addition formula directly.

For instance, $0{,}8\,c$ has $\varphi = \ln 3$. Twice $\ln 3$ is $\ln 9$, and $\tanh(\ln 9) = (81 - 1)/(81 + 1) = 80/82 \approx 0{,}976$. Rapidities can add without bound, yet $\tanh$ never reaches 1.
+++

bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: Solving $0{,}9 = \dfrac{0{,}8 + v}{1 + 0{,}8\,v}$ gives $v = 0{,}1/0{,}28 \approx 0{,}36\,c$. Check the calculation in the data panel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Consider a pair of twins. The stay-at-home twin follows the vertical white line. The traveling twin (pink line) flies to Alpha Centauri, $L = 4{,}37$ light-years away, at $0{,}8\,c$ and then returns. Each dot marks a birthday counted by the clock carried along that person’s path: this is {{thời gian riêng|proper time}}.

- The twin at home waits $T = 2L/v = 2 \times 4{,}37/0{,}8 \approx 10{,}9$ years.
- The traveling twin ages by $T/\gamma = 10{,}9/1{,}667 \approx 6{,}6$ years.

Proper time is the “length” of a world line, measured by $\Delta\tau = \sqrt{\Delta t^2 - \Delta x^2/c^2}$. The traveler’s bent world line has **less** proper time than the straight world line of the twin at home, even though it looks longer on paper. In ordinary geometry, a straight line is the **shortest** path between two points. In spacetime, a straight (unaccelerated) world line is the path of **longest** proper time.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the pink turnaround dot sideways to change the travel speed. Listen: each birthday at home sounds a low tone on the left, and each traveler birthday sounds a high tone on the right, spaced farther apart. Then view the trip in the outbound frame and in the inbound frame. In either frame, the other twin’s clock runs slower—yet no single inertial frame covers the traveler’s entire journey: to come home, the traveler must switch frames.
> [[Outbound frame|di]] [[Inbound frame|ve]] [[Home frame|nha]] [[Fly at 0.99 c|b99]] [[Alpha Centauri at 0.8 c|alpha]]

That resolves the {{nghịch lý anh em sinh đôi|twin paradox}}. The two twins are **not symmetric**: the traveler must accelerate at the turnaround, whereas the stay-at-home twin never leaves a single inertial frame. The two dashed lines mark the traveler’s “now” just before and just after turning around. They intersect the home twin’s world line nearly 7 years apart—years of the home twin’s life that sweep past the traveler’s “now” during the frame switch.

+++ Go deeper: proper time on each leg
Set $c = 1$ and measure time in years. The outbound leg has $\Delta t = L/\beta = 5{,}4625$ years and $\Delta x = 4{,}37$:

$$ \Delta\tau = \sqrt{5{,}4625^2 - 4{,}37^2} = 5{,}4625\sqrt{1 - 0{,}64} = 5{,}4625 \times 0{,}6 \approx 3{,}28 \text{ năm} $$

The return leg is identical, totaling $6{,}55$ years. At home, $\Delta x = 0$, so $\Delta\tau = \Delta t = 10{,}925$ years.

Just before turnaround, the traveler’s “now” is a line $t = \beta x + \text{hằng số}$, meeting the home world line at $L/\beta - \beta L \approx 1{,}97$ years. Just after turnaround, that line flips to $t = -\beta x + \text{hằng số}$, meeting it at $L/\beta + \beta L \approx 8{,}96$ years. The jump $2\beta L \approx 6{,}99$ years accounts for the missing time: the traveler sees the home twin age slowly on both legs, plus a sudden jump in simultaneous home age upon turning around.

bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
Here the horizontal axis shows **altitude** (2 km per grid division) and the vertical axis is $ct$. A muon created high in the atmosphere plunges downward at $0{,}998\,c$. Muons decay spontaneously with a mean rest lifetime of $\tau_0 = 2{,}197$ microseconds, during which light travels only $c\tau_0 = 659$ m. In Newtonian physics, most muons would decay after about 659 m (red ✗).

At $0{,}998\,c$, however, $\gamma = 15{,}8$. Seen from the ground, the muon’s internal clock runs 15.8 times slower, allowing it to travel an average of $\gamma\beta c\tau_0 \approx 10{,}4$ km. Rossi and Hall (1941) counted muons at two different altitudes and confirmed this prediction.

> [Thử ngay] Switch to the muon’s frame: the muon sits at rest and lives its normal 2.2 microseconds. The 10.4 km layer of atmosphere is length-contracted to just 657 m, and the ground rushes upward to meet it. Two frames, two explanations, one physical outcome: the muon reaches the ground.
> [[View from the muon|muon]] [[View from the ground|dat]]

> [Lưu ý] In the diagram, the muon is created at an altitude of 10.4 km for clarity—matching its mean travel distance, so it reaches the ground just as its own clock reads $\tau_0$.

### Other precision tests

- **Muons in the CERN storage ring** (Bailey et al., 1977): at $\gamma = 29{,}3$, their mean lifetime stretched to $29{,}3 \times 2{,}197 \approx 64{,}4$ microseconds, agreeing with special relativity to about one part in a thousand.
- **GPS**: satellites orbit at $3{,}87$ km/s, so their onboard clocks lose $v^2/(2c^2) \times 86\,400$ s $\approx 7{,}2$ microseconds per day from motion alone. (Gravity produces an opposite, larger shift: Lesson 9.)
- **LHC**: protons accelerated to 6.5 TeV with a rest mass of 0.938 GeV have $\gamma = E/mc^2 \approx 6\,928$, flying slower than $c$ by only about one part in a hundred million.

+++ Go deeper: four-velocity and E = mc²
Differentiating spacetime coordinates along a world line with respect to proper time gives the {{vận tốc bốn chiều|four-velocity}} $u = (\dd(ct)/\dd\tau,\ \dd x/\dd\tau) = \gamma\,(c,\ v)$. Its squared “length” is universal: $-u_t^2 + u_x^2 = \gamma^2(-c^2 + v^2) = -c^2$. Everything moves through spacetime at “speed” $c$; moving fast through space leaves less motion along proper time.

Multiplying by mass $m$ gives the {{xung lượng bốn chiều|four-momentum}} $p = m u = (\gamma m c,\ \gamma m v)$. Its time component times $c$ is energy: $E = \gamma m c^2$. At rest, $\gamma = 1$ and $E = mc^2$: mass is rest energy. At the LHC, $\gamma = 6\,500\ \text{GeV}/0{,}938\ \text{GeV}$.

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: Equals 1 at rest; 1.25 at 0.6 c; 5/3 at 0.8 c; grows without bound as v approaches c.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: Transforms the coordinates of the same event to a frame moving at speed v along x; y and z stay unchanged.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $\Delta\tau$: proper time of a moving clock. $L_0$: proper length, measured when the ruler is at rest.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: Identical in every inertial frame. Along a world line, $\Delta\tau = \sqrt{-s^2}/c$ is the proper time.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Two speeds below c always combine to less than c. Equivalent to adding rapidities: $\varphi_w = \varphi_u + \varphi_v$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.6.y: The time component of the four-momentum.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A spaceship flies past Earth at 0.8 c. A clock aboard the ship records 3 hours. How much time elapses for that interval as measured from Earth?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: γ(0.8) = 5/3, so Δt = γΔτ = 5/3 × 3 = 5 hours. Getting 1.8 hours comes from multiplying by 0.6 instead of dividing—reversing the frames. Moving clocks run slow, so the stationary frame measures a **longer** elapsed time.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Two events occur simultaneously at two separate places in the laboratory frame. A spaceship flies along the line from event A toward event B. According to the ship, what happens?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: It depends on where the observer sits on the ship
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The ship’s “now” sheet tilts upward in the direction of motion ($ct = \beta x$). Because B lies ahead, it sits below that sheet—in the ship’s past—so B happens first. This does not depend on where anyone sits: it is a statement about synchronized frame coordinates, not light-travel delay to an eye.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: A ruler of proper length 10 m flies past lengthwise at 0.6 c. What length does a stationary observer measure?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: L = L₀/γ = 10/1.25 = 8 m. Answering 12.5 m multiplies by γ instead of dividing, while 6 m multiplies by 0.6 (confusing β with 1/γ).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: From a ship flying at 0.6 c, an object is fired forward at 0.6 c relative to the ship. How fast does the object move relative to the ground?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: w = (0.6 + 0.6)/(1 + 0.36) = 1.2/1.36 ≈ 0.882 c. Newtonian addition gives 1.2 c, exceeding the speed of light, so it cannot be right.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: In the twin paradox, why can’t we flip the argument and claim that “from the traveler’s viewpoint, the stay-at-home twin was the one moving and should therefore be younger”?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.dap: Because the two twins are not symmetric. The stay-at-home twin remains in a single inertial frame the entire time, tracing a straight world line. The traveling twin must accelerate to turn around, giving a bent world line that switches from the outbound inertial frame to the inbound one. During each leg, the traveler really does measure the home clock running slow; however, during the frame switch, the traveler’s tilted “now” sweeps across a large stretch of the home twin’s world line (nearly 7 years in the Alpha Centauri trip). Accounting for that jump, the traveler ends up younger. In spacetime, a straight world line maximizes proper time.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: A muon at rest lives an average of 2.2 microseconds. A muon travels at 0.998 c (γ ≈ 15.8). From the muon’s own frame, how does it manage to cross more than 10 km of atmosphere?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: In the muon’s frame, its clock runs at its normal rate and it lives only about 2.2 microseconds. However, the atmosphere rushes upward toward it at 0.998 c, so the 10.4 km air column (measured from the ground) is length-contracted by a factor of γ to about 657 m. The ground arrives within 2.2 microseconds. Ground observers explain the survival via time dilation, while the muon explains it via length contraction—two consistent descriptions of the same event.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: E. F. Taylor and J. A. Wheeler, *Spacetime Physics* (2nd ed., 1992), chapter 3 on the principle of relativity, chapter 4 on a trip to Canopus (the twin paradox), and chapter 5 on proper time.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapters 4 and 5: Lorentz transformations, four-velocity, and four-momentum.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: R. P. Feynman, *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, Vol. I, chapter 15 “The Special Theory of Relativity” and chapter 16.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: A. Einstein, *Relativity: The Special and the General Theory* (1916), Part I: the train, the embankment, and the relativity of simultaneity.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A foundational statement accepted as a starting point. Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and the speed of light is the same for every observer.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: An idealized clock made of two parallel mirrors with a light pulse bouncing between them; each round trip is one tick. It lets us derive time dilation using nothing more than the Pythagorean theorem.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: The “hyperbolic rotation” angle $\varphi$ corresponding to velocity via $v/c = \tanh\varphi$. Rapidities of collinear frame boosts simply add.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: A twin who flies away and returns ends up younger than the twin who stayed home. There is no contradiction: the traveler changes inertial frames, while the twin at home does not.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: $p = m u = (\gamma m c,\ \gamma m \vec v)$. Its time component times $c$ is energy $E = \gamma m c^2$, which reduces at rest to $E = mc^2$.
